title: Sawmills of British Columbia
hook: in the early 1900s Sikh men worked sawmills and railways on Canada's west coast

segments.voice: Yesterday, leaving Punjab: police in Hong Kong, railway builders in East Africa, and your line, carrying the guru abroad. Today some of those men keep going east, across the Pacific, into the forests of Canada. Day three hundred fourteen.

Wet cedar, wood smoke, the scream of the blade: a sawmill in the rain. It's about 1906, on the coast of British Columbia. On the mill floor, among the other workers, are men in turbans, a long way from the wheat fields of Punjab. Some had heard about Canada in Hong Kong, where the ships for Vancouver set out. The pay was good, the work was hard, and the forests seemed endless. Today: the sawmills of British Columbia.
screen: `WET CEDAR AND WOOD SMOKE.` → `TURBANS ON THE MILL FLOOR.` → `ABOUT 1906.`

segments.voice: In the first years of the 1900s, a few thousand men from Punjab, nearly all of them Sikh, arrived on Canada's west coast. They worked in sawmills and logging camps, cleared land and laid track for the railways. It was heavy, dangerous work, often for lower pay than other workers got. And they met hostility. Many white residents wanted Asian immigrants kept out. In 1907, British Columbia took away the vote from people of South Asian origin. From 1908, Canada used a rule that immigrants had to arrive by a continuous journey from their home country, a rule that was almost impossible to meet from India. Immigration nearly stopped. The men who were already there held on. They lived together to save money, sent pay home, and did what Sikhs do: they built gurdwaras. In Vancouver in 1908, the Khalsa Diwan Society opened one of the first gurdwaras in North America. In 1911, Sikhs in Abbotsford, nearby, built a gurdwara with lumber from the mills and their own hands, and it still stands today, the oldest surviving gurdwara in North America. A Sikh mill owner later even founded a whole mill town on Vancouver Island and named it Paldi, after his village in Punjab. Behind all of it is an old Sikh value you already know: kirat karni, earning an honest living by your own work. Guru Nanak farmed. These men milled lumber. Honest work, far away, done with the Guru close by.
screen: `A FEW THOUSAND MEN FROM PUNJAB.` · `HOSTILITY, AND A CLOSED DOOR.` · `GURDWARAS BUILT FROM MILL LUMBER.` · `KIRAT KARNI: HONEST WORK.` · then, large: `HONEST WORK, FAR AWAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: thank a worker you rarely see. Settle, and breathe. Look around you and pick one thing: the chair, the table, the walls, the paper. Somewhere, someone cut the tree, ran the machine, drove the truck, stacked the boards. You'll never meet them. Picture their hands for a moment, and their tired evening after a long shift. If you pray, you can hold them in your prayer. If not, just send them a silent thank you. The bell holds the time.
Kirat. Honest labor — in the early 1900s, Sikh men did it in the mills and railways of Canada's west coast, and built gurdwaras from the lumber.
Your line: honest work, far away. Today, say a real thank you to one worker you usually pass without a word. Day three hundred fourteen.

howItsDone: Sikhs speak of kirat karni, honest work, as one of the three pillars of Sikh life; in Canada, the early mill workers' gurdwaras in Vancouver and Abbotsford are remembered as the community's beginnings.

original.note: Gurmukhi: kirat, honest labor; kirat karni, earning a living by your own work.

trapdoor: what you thought: early Sikh immigrants just came for the money.
what it means: they came for honest work, met a closed door, and built gurdwaras from the lumber they milled.
what a scholar hears: Canada's continuous journey regulation (1908) and British Columbia's 1907 disenfranchisement shaped the community for decades; the vote returned in 1947.
